caption_hook: Michigan has Great Lakes carved by ice, buried salt, fossil coral and some of the oldest rock in America.

layers.name: GLACIAL DRIFT
layers.hook: Ice scraped out the Great Lakes
layers.what: Mile-thick ice sheets bulldozed the land, then melted and left sand, gravel and clay across the state. The meltwater filled basins the ice had gouged deep.
layers.bonus: Michigan touches four of the five Great Lakes, all gouged out by ice.

layers.name: TRAVERSE GROUP
layers.what: A warm, shallow sea teemed with honeycomb corals. Their fossils are packed into this limestone, and glaciers later scattered the pieces along Lake Michigan beaches.
layers.bonus: The fossil coral Petoskey stone is Michigan's official state stone.

layers.name: SALINA SALT
layers.what: A sea cut off from the ocean slowly evaporated, leaving thick beds of rock salt. They lie buried deep under the middle of Michigan and the Detroit region.
layers.bonus: Miles of tunnels run beneath Detroit, over 1,000 feet down, mined for road salt.

layers.name: MUNISING SANDSTONE
layers.what: Beach sand from an ancient shoreline hardened into sandstone. Along Lake Superior, waves have carved it into arches, caves and cliffs up to 200 feet tall.
layers.bonus: Seeping groundwater stains the cliffs red, orange, green and black with minerals.

layers.name: PORTAGE LAKE LAVA
layers.hook: Lava pockets full of pure copper
layers.what: When the continent tried to split, lava flooded the Keweenaw Peninsula. Hot fluids later filled gas bubbles and cracks in it with nearly pure copper metal.
layers.bonus: People mined this native copper for thousands of years before Europeans arrived.

layers.name: WATERSMEET GNEISS
layers.hook: The oldest known rock in the U.S.
layers.what: Deep-crust rock squeezed and baked into striped gneiss. Studies of the Watersmeet area in the Upper Peninsula date it to at least 3.6 billion years old.
layers.bonus: That is nearly four-fifths of the way back to when Earth formed.
